newsitem.title: CHINA: China secondary copper imports seen threatened.
newsitem.headline: China secondary copper imports seen threatened.

text.p: A potential ban on exports of some secondary raw materials from most OECD member countries could slash China's secondary copper imports from 1998, a U.S. Chamber of Commerce official said on Tuesday.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development is considering an export ban on some materials under the Basle Convention to prevent the dumping of harmful waste in the developing world.
"China would be hurt," said Harvey Alter, manager of the resources policy department of the U.S. Chamber, a grouping of U.S. businesses.
He was speaking at the 32nd World Congress of the International Chamber of Commerce, currently being held in Shanghai.
The export ban under the Basle Convention would take effect on January 1, 1998 if it is ratified by a majority of OECD members. The US is not party to the convention.
"China needs copper. Certain forms of secondary copper cannot come into the country (if the convention is approved)," Alter said.
"China can also buy primary copper on the market at a much higher price and shut down smelters," he said.
Alter gave no details, but China's official customs figures show total copper scrap imports in 1995 were 300,000 tonnes.
China also imports secondary aluminium and steel, but such metals would not be affected by the convention, Alter said.
Alter said the convention would in effect become a trade barrier for countries that needed secondary raw materials to help their economic development.
Peter Netchaef, general manager of Australia's Simetal Ltd, said the ban would only hurt end-users of secondary metals as developed countries would probably absorb the surplus for their own use.
